title: The stones became one (Genesis Rabbah 68:11)
hookLine: stones quarrel over who will be Jacob's pillow, and become one stone
tomorrow: same night, a ladder. why is Jacob scared to climb it?

cards: Two siblings, one back seat, one armrest: a whole war over a few inches of plastic. Genesis has a stranger quarrel, hidden in the grammar. Jacob, running from his brother, stops for the night.
In the King James wording, "he took of the stones of that place, and put them for his pillows." Stones, plural. Next morning he "took the stone that he had put for his pillows."
One stone. Where did the rest go?

teach.b: Genesis Rabbah has an answer, one of the midrashim you could tell a kid at bedtime. The stones started quarreling. Each one said: let this righteous man lay his head on me.
On me, not you. And in the night, the Holy One made them one stone, so nobody lost. Notice what the stones are fighting about.
Not about being left out, or stuck with the job.

Each one wants to be the one that serves. It's a quarrel between good intentions, the kind families have all the time: two people who both want to host the holiday, two siblings who both want to drive Dad to the doctor.
And the midrash doesn't pick a winner. No stone is told: you were right. They're joined, and the head rests on all of them at once.
The grammar puzzle has a story behind it. The plural turns singular because something happened in the night, and the midrash fills that gap with peace.
It sits right before the ladder, too.
Before Jacob dreams of heaven, the ground under his head stops fighting.

how: Genesis Rabbah 68:11 is studied with the Torah portion Vayetze, which opens with Jacob's night on the road; the stones are a favorite story in Jewish children's retellings.

games.q: what does “the stones became one” mean?
o: a stone wall built to keep his brother out
a heap of rocks Jacob piled up as an altar
rivals who both wanted to serve, joined in peace

games.q: the stones, plural and singular — tap the pairs.
p: what Jacob puts under his head
what he lifts in the morning
let him rest his head on me

s: the stones fought because none of them wanted the job
each one wanted to be the one Jacob rested on.
the midrash starts from a change between plural and singular
stones at night, the stone in the morning.
in the midrash, God picks the best stone
no winner: they're made into one.

games.q: two friends both want to throw your birthday dinner, and both mean well. by the stones, what's the move?
o: flip a coin; someone has to lose for it to be fair.
ask them to host it together, so both hands are in it.
pick the one who asked first; that settles it fastest.
games.why: in Genesis Rabbah no stone is told it won. they're joined, and the head rests on all of them.

practice: Bring to mind one small quarrel you're in, where both of you want something good. Version a text to that person, in your head or on your phone without sending: one line that names what you both want.
Let it sit there for the rest of the sit; whether it goes is for later.

wordCard.voice: The stones became one: the midrash's answer to Genesis 28. Stones that fought over who would serve, joined in the night.

orig.note: Hebrew: stone. Genesis 28 moves from stones to the stone.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the stones became one, and nobody had to lose. See you tomorrow.
